guided.title: Add a category
guided.prompt: Insert a new row into `categories` with `category_name` `Snacks` and `description` `Chips and nuts`, leaving `category_id` to the database. End the statement with `RETURNING category_id, category_name` so the result shows the generated id and the name.
guided.starter:
-- Insert the category 'Snacks' and return its id and name
SELECT category_id, category_name
FROM categories
WHERE category_name = 'Snacks';
hints: The starter only reads the table. A new row needs an INSERT statement.
INSERT INTO categories (category_name, description) VALUES (...); do not list category_id.
Add RETURNING category_id, category_name after the VALUES list.

guided.title: Add two shippers at once
guided.prompt: Insert two rows into `shippers` with one statement: `Northern Freight` with phone `555-0101`, and `Coastal Haulage` with a NULL phone. Return `shipper_id`, `company_name` and `phone` with `RETURNING`.
guided.starter:
-- Insert two shippers in one statement and return them
INSERT INTO shippers (company_name, phone)
VALUES ('Northern Freight', '555-0101')
RETURNING shipper_id, company_name, phone;
guided.solution:
INSERT INTO shippers (company_name, phone)
VALUES ('Northern Freight', '555-0101'),
       ('Coastal Haulage', NULL)
RETURNING shipper_id, company_name, phone;
hints: The starter inserts only the first shipper. Add a second value list.
Separate the value lists with a comma: VALUES (...), (...). A missing phone is the keyword NULL.

guided.title: Cut meat prices by 10 percent
guided.prompt: Update the products of category 6 so that `unit_price` becomes 90 percent of its current value, rounded to 2 decimals. Return `product_id`, `product_name` and the new `unit_price` with `RETURNING`.
guided.starter:
-- Reduce the price of category 6 products by 10 percent
UPDATE products
SET unit_price = unit_price
WHERE category_id = 6
RETURNING product_id, product_name, unit_price;
guided.solution:
UPDATE products
SET unit_price = ROUND(unit_price * 0.90, 2)
WHERE category_id = 6
RETURNING product_id, product_name, unit_price;
hints: The starter sets each price to itself, so nothing changes. The new value must be computed from the old one.
Multiply the current price by 0.90 and wrap it in ROUND(..., 2).

guided.title: Remove single-unit lines
guided.prompt: Delete the rows of `order_details` whose `quantity` is exactly 1, then, in a second statement, return the number of lines left as `lines_left` with `SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_left FROM order_details`.
guided.starter:
-- Delete lines with quantity 1, then count the lines left
SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_left FROM order_details;
hints: The starter only counts. Put a DELETE statement before the SELECT, ended by a semicolon.
Without the WHERE clause every line would be deleted.

independent.title: Mark old unshipped orders as shipped
independent.prompt: For orders that have no `shipped_date` and were placed before 1996-06-01, set `shipped_date` to three days after `order_date` (a date plus an integer adds days). Return `order_id`, `order_date` and `shipped_date` with `RETURNING`.
independent.starter:
-- Set shipped_date = order_date + 3 for old unshipped orders
SELECT order_id, order_date, shipped_date
FROM orders
WHERE shipped_date IS NULL AND order_date < '1996-06-01';
independent.solution:
UPDATE orders
SET shipped_date = order_date + 3
WHERE shipped_date IS NULL AND order_date < '1996-06-01'
RETURNING order_id, order_date, shipped_date;

independent.title: Create backup shippers
independent.prompt: Insert one new shipper for every existing shipper, using `INSERT ... SELECT`. The new `company_name` is the old name followed by ` (backup)` (text joined with `||`), and `phone` is copied. Return `shipper_id` and `company_name` of the new rows with `RETURNING`.
independent.starter:
-- Copy each shipper as '<name> (backup)'
INSERT INTO shippers (company_name, phone)
VALUES ('Speedy Express (backup)', NULL)
RETURNING shipper_id, company_name;
independent.solution:
INSERT INTO shippers (company_name, phone)
SELECT company_name || ' (backup)', phone
FROM shippers
RETURNING shipper_id, company_name;

independent.title: Reactivate unsold products
independent.prompt: Stretch task. Set `discontinued` to false and reduce `unit_price` by 10 percent (rounded to 2 decimals) for the products that are currently discontinued and never appear in `order_details` (use a subquery with `NOT IN`). Return `product_id`, `product_name`, `discontinued` and the new `unit_price` with `RETURNING`.
independent.starter:
-- Reactivate discontinued products that were never ordered
SELECT product_id, product_name, discontinued, unit_price
FROM products
WHERE discontinued AND product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_details);
independent.solution:
UPDATE products
SET discontinued = false,
    unit_price = ROUND(unit_price * 0.90, 2)
WHERE discontinued
  AND product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_details)
RETURNING product_id, product_name, discontinued, unit_price;

checks.question: What does `UPDATE products SET unit_price = 0;` (no WHERE) do?
options: Nothing, because UPDATE requires a WHERE clause
Sets the price of every product to 0
Sets the price of the first product to 0
Fails with a syntax error
checks.explanation: WHERE is optional in UPDATE and DELETE. Without it every row is changed, and the database reports success. That is why you write and test the WHERE as a SELECT first.

checks.question: A table has columns `company_name` (NOT NULL, no default) and `phone`. What happens with `INSERT INTO shippers (phone) VALUES ('555')`?
options: A row is inserted with an empty company name
A row is inserted with company_name NULL
It fails with a not-null constraint violation
It inserts the phone into the first column
checks.explanation: company_name has no default and may not be NULL, so the database rejects the row with 'null value in column company_name violates not-null constraint'. Naming columns explicitly means the phone goes to the phone column, not the first column.

checks.question: The shippers table holds ids 1 to 3. After `INSERT INTO shippers (company_name) VALUES ('A'), ('B') RETURNING shipper_id`, which ids are returned (the sequence starts fresh)?
options: 1 and 2
3 and 4
4 and 5
NULL and NULL
checks.explanation: shipper_id is a generated serial column, so the sequence supplies the next unused numbers, 4 and 5. The ids 1 to 3 already exist. RETURNING shows the generated values.

checks.question: Why does `DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 'ALFKI'` fail in Northwind?
options: customer_id cannot be used in WHERE
ALFKI has orders, and the foreign key from orders to customers forbids deleting a referenced row
DELETE needs a RETURNING clause
Only the last customer can be deleted
checks.explanation: orders.customer_id references customers.customer_id. While ALFKI has orders, deleting the customer would leave orphan orders, so PostgreSQL rejects the statement with a foreign key violation.

checks.question: What does `UPDATE t SET a = b, b = a` do to a row where a = 1 and b = 2?
options: Sets both columns to 1
Sets both columns to 2
Swaps them: a becomes 2 and b becomes 1
Fails because a column is used twice
checks.explanation: All right-hand expressions are evaluated using the old values of the row before any assignment, so a gets the old b (2) and b gets the old a (1). The columns are swapped.

checks.question: Which is the best first step before running a risky `DELETE FROM order_details WHERE quantity < 3`?
options: Run it and look at the message
Run SELECT * FROM order_details WHERE quantity < 3 to see exactly which rows it would remove
Remove the WHERE clause so nothing is missed
Add RETURNING, because it undoes the delete
checks.explanation: A SELECT with the same WHERE shows the rows and the count the DELETE would affect. RETURNING only reports what was deleted after the fact and does not undo anything. Removing the WHERE clause would delete every line.
